you don't.

## Output

Say less, mean more. Lead with the answer, then only the reasoning that changes a decision.

- No preamble, no restating the task, no closing summary of what you just did.
- Status ≤4 lines. Technical explanation ≤8. Design rationale ≤15. Longer than that → table or

- Code, commands, errors, and diffs verbatim. File references as `path:line`.
- Uncertainty gets one line stating what would settle it — not a paragraph of hedging.
- Report outcomes faithfully. Tests failed → say so with the output. Step skipped → say so.
  Done and verified → say it plainly, without hedging.

## Code

Climb this ladder before writing anything, in order. Stop at the first rung that works:

1. Is it needed at all?
2. Already in this codebase? Reuse it.
3. Standard library?
4. Platform primitive?
5. A dependency already installed?
6. A one-liner?
7. The minimum that works.

Climb it *after* understanding the problem — read the code and trace the real flow first.

- Deletion beats addition. Boring beats clever. Fewest files, shortest diff.
- No unrequested abstractions. No scaffolding for a future that hasn't arrived.
- Fix root causes. Find every caller before changing shared behaviour; fix the shared function
  once rather than patching each site.
- Consolidate near-duplicate logic. One change should mean one edit in one place.
- Comment only what the code cannot say: constraints, invariants, why-not-the-obvious-way.
  Never narrate what the next line does.

where the failure loses data, security, accessibility.

Nothing is done because it looks done.

- Run it. A change that compiles is not a change that works.

  confident one. Confidence and correctness are uncorrelated.
- When a result surprises you, suspect the measurement before the conclusion.

Judge each piece of work as either **routine** or **consequential**, and say which in one line.

architecture, anything spanning systems, anything where the obvious answer is probably wrong.

  parallel workers, use genuinely separate ones and let them disagree; where it doesn't,

  the same review three times. Redundancy catches slips; diversity catches blind spots.

Verified: exit 0, one request, providerServed=DeepInfra, 6172 promptTokens for 'reply with exactly: ok'. CONTAINER: bench/opencode:pinned (opencode-ai@1.18.18, warmed npm cache so the per-run plugin install works offline). Containerized promptTokens 7329 vs 6172 native, i.e. HIGHER: OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR did NOT stop native opencode reading ~/.config/opencode — it loaded the user global AGENTS.md and a user orchestrator agent that replaces the system prompt and drops the edit/write tools (8 tools native vs 10 stock). The container gets stock opencode. AGENTS.md planted: byte-identical body. BASELINE INSTRUCTION FILE (spec/baseline.md): corpus/AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md is materialised into the workdir as AGENTS.md, byte-identical for every harness; config `instructions` flipped from [] to ["AGENTS.md"] — that key is workspace-only, so every OPENCODE_PURE / OPENCODE_DISABLE_* host-suppression var is untouched. OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG had to be REMOVED as well: with it set, `instructions` is never read and a workdir AGENTS.md is invisible (proved against a logging sink — request body 9,791 B with the var, 14,196 B without it, same 10 tools). It is workspace-scoped (project-level opencode.json / .opencode / instructions), so removing it does not re-open host state: OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR, OPENCODE_PURE, OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS/EXTERNAL_SKILLS/CLAUDE_CODE(_SKILLS/_PROMPT) and the container empty HOME all stay. Consequence to know: a corpus task that shipped its own opencode.json or .opencode dir would now be honoured; none do.

label: Hermes
notes: Wired with --provider custom + CUSTOM_BASE_URL (env, consulted unconditionally ahead of config in hermes_cli/runtime_provider.py) plus a per-run config.yaml carrying the same base_url. OPENAI_API_KEY=bench-dummy is the key hermes picks for a non-OpenRouter custom endpoint, so the real OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the runner's env is never handed to the harness. HERMES_HOME is redirected into the workdir, so ~/.hermes/config.yaml, ~/.hermes/.env, sessions, memory, SOUL.md and skills are untouched and cannot bias the run (verified: 'hermes prompt-size' reports 0 B skills index / 0 B memory / 0 B AGENTS.md context). Fairness flags: -z is inherently non-interactive and auto-bypasses approvals, --yolo bypasses dangerous-command prompts, --accept-hooks auto-approves unseen shell hooks, --ignore-rules skips AGENTS.md / SOUL.md / memory injection. auxiliary.title_generation.enabled=false is a COST setting: by default hermes fires a second billed call to title the session (observed 237 prompt / 282 completion tokens). Verified: exit 0, one /chat/completions request, providerServed=DeepInfra, 13352 promptTokens for 'reply with exactly: ok'. Two caveats to carry into the report: (1) hermes also probes GET /v1/models and /v1/models/<id> at startup (3-4 passthrough rows per run, 0 tokens, providerServed null — summary.ts will flag them as pin violations unless non-completion paths are excluded); (2) hermes exits 0 even when the model call fails outright (observed on an upstream 429: stdout carried 'API call failed after 3 retries' and exit was still 0), so grade hermes on verify.sh + the usage file's completed/failed fields, never on exit code. (3) METERING GAP: in 2 of 4 verification runs hermes returned the right answer with exit 0 and a populated --usage-file (13,349 input incl. 13,056 cache-read), yet the proxy wrote NO row for that /chat/completions call — every time, the run had hit an upstream 429 first. Most likely hermes aborts the SSE stream once it has the final text, so the proxy's stream-end handler (where the usage row is written) never fires. Cross-check hermes runs against the per-run .bench-hermes-usage.json before trusting proxy token totals for this harness. CONTAINER: bench/hermes:pinned (git e02d1e4, uv sync --locked). Containerized promptTokens 12233 vs 13352 native: native injected Project Context from the user .cursor/rules/*.mdc and carried a browser_exec tool from the host playwright install; the image deliberately omits browser/computer-use (17 tools vs 18). AGENTS.md planted: byte-identical body. BASELINE INSTRUCTION FILE (spec/baseline.md): corpus/AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md is materialised into the workdir as AGENTS.md, byte-identical for every harness; --ignore-rules removed. It conflated workspace AGENTS.md with SOUL.md/memory injection and has no finer form; host state is still suppressed because HERMES_HOME points at a per-run dir inside the workdir and the container HOME is empty, so there is no SOUL.md or memory to inject. WARNING — THE BRIEFING DOES NOT REACH HERMES IN -z MODE. --ignore-rules was removed (it maps to skip_context_files/skip_memory) but the delta was exactly zero: `-z/--oneshot` takes hermes_cli/oneshot.py, which builds AIAgent directly and never passes (or honours) context-file loading at all, so --ignore-rules is INERT on this path and no AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/.cursorrules is ever injected. Proved against a logging sink with AGENTS.md present in cwd: -z system prompt 8,431 chars, no `# Project Context` block; the same container with `chat -q "..." -Q` produced 25,060 chars WITH the Project Context block and the file verbatim. So hermes CAN receive the briefing, but only by switching the invocation from `-z` to `chat -q`, which also changes the measured harness (18 tools instead of 17, session persistence back on, --usage-file is a top-level flag not available on chat, and the title-generation/second-call analysis would need redoing). That switch is deliberately NOT applied here — it is a harness-configuration decision, not an instruction-delivery one. --ignore-rules stays removed because it is a no-op under -z and is the prerequisite for the chat -q path.
